Remember the distinction: electronics engineers determine how circuits operate, while software and embedded engineers determine how code operates. One defines the hardware; the other defines the logic.

This occupation is a poor fit for people who fear soldering, cannot tolerate exacting specifications, or feel overwhelmed by waveforms. Electronics engineers often work late debugging signals and revise boards repeatedly, so patience matters.

A common path is: bachelor's degree in electronics, communications, or electrical engineering → hardware assistant or test role → independent board and module design → project ownership → system architecture or technical specialist.
This occupation suits people who enjoy hardware, think analytically, can debug boards, and can carry projects. It fits people who value circuits that are stable, cost-efficient, and compact.

Electronics Engineers, Except Computer lead the design of electronic systems, circuits, and equipment. They coordinate schematics, PCB design, embedded systems, and controls; use simulation and test tools; deliver production-ready designs; and support pilot production.

paragraphs: In the morning, engineers align interface timing with firmware teams and update schematics. Later, they route in EDA, run signal-integrity simulations, and check power ripple and cooling. Before pilot production, they review packaging and processes through several revisions. They solder prototypes and compare measurements in the laboratory, document corrective actions, and prepare board-change lists for the next review.

In one sentence: they turn requirements into working circuits. They develop concepts, draw schematics, lay out PCBs, run simulations, support pilot production, and balance performance with cost. The work combines analysis and hands-on debugging, with electronics engineers leading hardware design.

paragraphs: A score of 7/10 places this occupation in the moderate-high exposure range for hardware design. Systems accelerate routing and checking, while people retain responsibility for architecture and coordination.

Moderate-high exposure does not mean high job risk. AI replaces routine board layout and error checking, not system-architecture roles. Engineers who can shape architecture, align teams, and oversee production become scarcer as tools improve. Assistants limited to routine boards face the greatest pressure.
